en: Dhātukathā 2 Niddesa 2.7.
Exposition of the Seventh Method: The Exposition of the Terms for the Associated and the Dissociated.

Those phenomena that are included in the aggregate of feeling … those phenomena that are included in the aggregate of perception … those phenomena that are included in the aggregate of mental formations …

Regarding those phenomena associated with the aggregate of consciousness (viññāṇakkhandha) … and those phenomena associated with the mind base (manāyatana), as to those phenomena dissociated from them: by how many aggregates, by how many bases, and by how many elements are those phenomena dissociated?
Those phenomena are dissociated from four aggregates, from one base, and from seven elements.
They are dissociated from one base and from one element by some [factors].
Those phenomena associated with the eye-consciousness-element …pe… those phenomena associated with the mind-element …
Those phenomena which are dissociated from those phenomena associated with the mind-consciousness element (manoviññāṇadhātu) … those phenomena are dissociated from none of the aggregates (khandha),

none of the bases (āyatana), and from one element (dhātu). Those phenomena which are dissociated from those phenomena associated with the mind-faculty (manindriya) … [are likewise dissociated from none of the aggregates, none of the bases, and from one element].
Those phenomena are dissociated from four aggregates, one base, and seven elements;
they are dissociated from one base and one element with respect to certain [other] phenomena.
Those phenomena which are dissociated from those phenomena that are associated with the equanimity faculty...
Those states are dissociated from none of the aggregates, none of the bases, and five of the elements.
Those states [arising] through the condition of volitional formations by way of consciousness...
those states [arising] through the condition of the sixfold base by way of contact...
Those phenomena [arising] with contact as condition for feeling;
those phenomena [arising] through contact;
those phenomena [arising] through feeling.
Those phenomena that are associated with perception … those phenomena that are associated with volition … those phenomena that are associated with consciousness …
Those phenomena which are dissociated from those phenomena associated with attention:
those phenomena are dissociated from four aggregates, one base, and seven elements;
they are dissociated from one base and one element in some respects.
Those phenomena which are associated with resolve (*adhimokkha*), and those phenomena which are dissociated from those [associated] phenomena...
those phenomena are dissociated from none of the aggregates (*khandha*), from none of the bases (*āyatana*), and from one element (*dhātu*).
Those phenomena which are associated with states associated with neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling (*adukkhamasukhā vedanā*)...

Those phenomena which are dissociated from those phenomena associated with states accompanied by equanimity… those phenomena are dissociated from none of the aggregates, none of the bases, and five elements.
Those phenomena which are dissociated from those phenomena associated with states accompanied by applied thought and sustained thought…
Those phenomena are dissociated from none of the aggregates, from none of the bases, and from one element.
Those phenomena which [are dissociated] from mental states… those phenomena which [are dissociated] from mental factors…
Those phenomena which [arise] through phenomena associated with consciousness;
those phenomena which [arise] through phenomena conjoined with consciousness;
those phenomena which [arise] through phenomena conjoined with and originated by consciousness.
Those phenomena which are dissociated from those phenomena that are conjoined with, originated by, and co-existent with the mind;
and those phenomena which are dissociated from those phenomena that are conjoined with, originated by, and follow upon the mind—
those phenomena are dissociated from four aggregates, one base, and seven elements.
They are dissociated from one base and from one element,
and from certain [other] factors.

Those factors which are associated with factors accompanied by initial application (*savitakka*)— those factors which are dissociated from those factors accompanied by sustained application (*savicāra*)...
Those phenomena are dissociated from none of the aggregates, from none of the bases, and from one element.

As for those phenomena that are dissociated from the phenomena associated with equanimity—how many aggregates, how many bases, and how many elements are those [dissociated] phenomena dissociated from?
Those phenomena are dissociated from none of the aggregates, from none of the bases, and from five elements.
Four aggregates, one base,
seven elements, and two faculties; likewise,
three conditions with contact as the fifth.
In the triads of mental application, there are three;
two are associated with the mind within the interval of the seven;
and there is the investigation of thought accompanied by equanimity. [37]
The seventh section is the exposition of the dissociated state by means of the associated state.
